note: Start with the high-value heavy end: isolate C7+, then heptane, and finally octane from nonane, using moderate energy duties.
Repurpose the train to recover the two highest-value products: make a sharp C7/C8 split at the feed, then separate octane from nonane.
Establish a sharp C7/C8 split with a smaller, lower-pressure column before spending solves on downstream separation.
Test a single-column nonane recovery: its high value can cover one column, while avoiding an unprofitable full separation train.
Recover octane and nonane with a two-column heavy-end train, using moderate reflux and boil-up to keep energy costs below their combined product value.
Restore a sharp C7/C8 feed split and then separate the valuable octane/nonane bottoms into two pure products.
Increase separation sharpness in the two-column heavy-end train so both octane and nonane reach saleable purity.
Shift the feed-column cut upward to send all C7+ material to the bottoms, then use the second column specifically for the octane/nonane split.
Test a lean single-column nonane recovery at full feed pressure: avoid refrigeration and high boil-up while retaining enough stages for a sharp C8/C9 split.
Build a blend-oriented flowsheet: recover C3, C4, C5 and C6-paraffin products while leaving the heavy end unsold, avoiding the unprofitable deep heavy-end separation.
Build a complete blend-and-heavy-products train: C3, C4 and C5 blends, then heptane, octane and nonane. This spreads column costs over most of the feed value instead of selling only C3.
Restore the best valid blend-oriented design and inspect its column-by-column economics before targeted improvement.
Rebuild the five-column blend train at full feed pressure to avoid refrigeration and excess pressure-drop cost, using moderate stages and reflux to target positive economics.
Focus on the two most valuable products: make a sharp C7/C8 feed split, then recover octane and nonane in one small heavy-end column.
Use a warm, full-pressure direct sequence: recover a C8+ bottoms cut first, then split it into high-purity octane and nonane products.
Sharpen the C7/C8 feed cut so the heavy column receives essentially only octane and nonane, then move its cut to recover both as pure products.
Test the simplest profitable option first: recover high-purity nonane directly in one full-pressure column, with a much lower boil-up duty than the C7/C8 split.
Target nonane as the single saleable bottoms product: set the feed-column cut between octane and nonane and reduce stages and boil-up to keep costs below its product value.
Drive the single feed column to a true octane/nonane split so the bottoms becomes premium nonane; the previous boil-up only stripped the C3 fraction.
Make a genuinely sharp octane/nonane split with enough rectification and stripping to sell premium nonane; the previous low reflux left nearly all octane in the bottoms.
Build a warm five-column train around the existing C5/C6 split: sell C3, C4 and C5 blends overhead, and recover premium octane and nonane from the heavy end.
Return to the cheapest potentially profitable scheme: one warm column recovering premium nonane, with substantially less capital and energy than the prior attempts.
Recover nonane in a single warm column with low boil-up and modest rectification; this targets the high-value heavy product while avoiding the excessive duties of earlier sharp-split attempts.
Raise stripping enough to move the cut to octane/nonane while retaining the modest 18-stage shell; this should finally isolate nonane as a saleable bottoms product.
Increase boil-up enough to move the cut down to octane/nonane while keeping a modest warm column; the target is premium nonane in a roughly 250 mol/s bottoms stream.
Make the one-column nonane recovery genuinely sharp: high stripping should put essentially all octane overhead while retaining nonane in a saleable bottoms stream.
Recover nonane in one low-pressure column, avoiding the very costly full-pressure refrigeration and extreme duties that made every prior design uneconomic.
Minimize the single-column nonane recovery duty: the warm, low-pressure shell needs only enough reflux and boil-up for the easy octane/nonane split, not the extreme flows used previously.

Build a warm, low-pressure blend-recovery train: C3 overhead, C4 from the second column, and C5 overhead from the third. Moderate duties and stage counts should produce three saleable blends without the extreme costs of pure-component recovery.
Return to the best one-product scheme and test the warmest allowable operation; lower pressure should cut refrigeration and utility costs while retaining the nonane recovery.

Recover the two highest-value heavy products with a warm heptane/octane split followed by an easy octane/nonane column; this should create two premium products rather than one low-purity bottoms stream.
Strip the light 92% of the feed overhead in a small warm column and sell the nonane-rich bottoms. The much smaller shell and duties should bring cost below the nonane product value.

Build a seven-column warm-train baseline selling the C3, C4, C5 and C6-paraffin blends plus octane and nonane. Moderate duties should reveal which separations and products are economic before further refinement.
Return to the strongest one-product route and minimize its shell and duties: a 16-stage warm column with low reflux and moderate stripping, targeting saleable nonane bottoms.
Increase stripping in the compact warm column to push octane and lighter material overhead while retaining nonane in a saleable bottoms product.
Test the smallest possible warm column with very strong stripping and minimal reflux, aiming to retain nonane while rejecting essentially all octane at much lower capital and utility cost.
Add rectification/stripping stages while keeping a warm low-pressure shell and modest duties, targeting >95% nonane bottoms with high recovery.

Reset to the zero-column baseline and test a single warm C3 product split. Moderate reflux and boil-up should give a saleable C3 blend without the extreme stripping duty that made nonane recovery uneconomic.

Test a compact two-column heavy-products route: first reject heptane and all lighter material overhead, then split octane from nonane. This adds the high-value octane product while keeping both columns warm and small.

Increase rectification and stripping for a sharp heptane/octane split followed by octane/nonane separation. Both warm columns target two high-value pure products, with enough stages to avoid the previous severe leakage.

Test the key cost hypothesis directly: operate at feed pressure so the condenser is warm rather than refrigerated. Use a compact, strongly stripped column to recover nonane as the sole high-value bottoms product.
Build a six-column warm train for C4/C5/C6 blends and heavy pure products. Moderate stages and duties avoid the extreme cost and convergence problems of earlier sharp-split attempts.

Concentrate on the two most valuable products with only two warm columns: reject heptane and lighter components overhead, then split octane from nonane. Moderate staging and reflux should give saleable purity without the extreme cost of the earlier sharp-split attempt.
Make a single warm, strongly stripped nonane column with enough stages for a sharp octane/nonane split. If purity exceeds 95%, its $404M/yr value should finally outweigh the column cost.
Test a genuinely rectifying octane/nonane split rather than extreme boil-up: 80 stages and reflux 8 should approach premium nonane while avoiding the very large stripping duty.

Build a compact warm sequential train that monetizes every major cut: ethane rejection, C3/C4/C5 blends, C6 paraffin blend, and pure octane/nonane. Moderate stage counts and duties should spread column costs over more than $2.3B/yr of product value.

Return to the simplest high-value route: one feed-pressure column making premium nonane bottoms. High rectification and strong stripping should remove the octane leakage that defeated earlier compact attempts.
Target a profitable single-product nonane column with much lower rectification cost than the failed 80–100 stage designs, while strong stripping limits the bottoms to the heaviest cut.
Reduce rectification and stripping duties in the best single-column nonane route. This tests whether a 95% nonane bottoms product can be obtained well below the prior column cost.

Optimize the warm single-column nonane route with balanced rectification and stripping. Sixty stages should sharpen the octane/nonane split while avoiding the extreme boil-up and reflux duties of earlier attempts.
Drive octane overhead much harder in the warm nonane column. The prior 60-stage split still left most octane in the bottoms, so a much larger boil-up is needed before further optimization.
Use a single warm three-product column: lights overhead, a small octane-rich liquid side draw, and nonane bottoms. This can monetize the two most valuable components without a second costly column.

A moderate pressure drop should improve the octane/nonane relative volatility while keeping the condenser warm. Test a shorter, lower-reflux column to bring the single-product nonane route below its revenue.

Switch to a low-duty, feed-pressure ethane/C3 separation. The C3 blend is worth about $302M/yr and the propane–isobutane split is easy, so two modest columns should have a much better value-to-cost ratio than the heavy-product routes.
Extend the warm-end recovery to the valuable C4 blend: take C4 overhead with the C3s, split C3/C4 in the second column, and retain the small ethane rejection column.
Restore the best valid C3-recovery design, then optimize its operating cost and recovery rather than adding a difficult propane/isobutane splitter.
The second column is inexpensive but sends 177 mol/s of valuable C3s overhead with ethane. Increase rectification to recover those C3s in the blend while retaining the efficient feed split.
The feed column leaves about 200 mol/s of valuable C3s in the worthless bottoms. Increase stripping to recover them overhead, while retaining the proven ethane-rejection column.
Restore the best valid two-column C3 recovery design before making a more controlled optimization.
Recover more of the valuable C3s from both the feed-column bottoms and the ethane overhead using modest increases in boil-up, while preserving the validated splits.
Reduce the expensive feed-column size and reflux while preserving the easy C3/C4 split. A slightly lighter ethane column should retain high C3 recovery at lower total cost.

The second column is inexpensive but still loses 234 mol/s overhead, including about 130 mol/s of valuable C3s. Increase stripping substantially to recover those C3s in the blend while retaining ethane overhead.
Restore the best low-cost C3 recovery design; excessive stripping in the ethane column increased losses and cost rather than improving blend recovery.
Increase feed-column stripping modestly to recover more of the roughly 100 mol/s of C3s currently lost to the bottoms, without repeating the excessive second-column stripping change.
The inexpensive ethane column still sends about 190 mol/s of C3s overhead. Test a modest reboil increase to recover them into the blend without repeating the excessive-stripping case.
Restore the best valid design before testing more targeted changes; the higher ethane-column boil-up reduced profit.
The feed-column bottoms still contain essentially all of the C4s, worth about $246M/yr as a blend. Add a modest C4/C5 split to recover that value while leaving the proven C3 section unchanged.
The added C4 column costs far more than the recovered blend is worth and loses most C4s to the tops. Restore the best two-column design before targeted optimization.

Test the much higher-value heavy-products route: isolate the C8/C9 cut at the feed, then split it into pure octane and nonane. Both separations are thermally easy and avoid the expensive refrigerated C3 condenser.
Restore the best C3 design and test a lower-pressure, lower-reflux ethane column. Easier C2/C3 separation may recover more blend with less energy despite the colder condenser.
Restore the best design and improve the inexpensive ethane/C3 split with more stages rather than more boil-up, aiming to recover the large C3 overhead loss without increasing vapour traffic.

Push the inexpensive ethane column toward a sharp C2/C3 split: the current overhead still contains about 143 mol/s of valuable C3s, so a substantially higher boil-up may both recover blend and produce saleable ethane.
Restore the best low-cost C3 blend design after the aggressive ethane-column settings sharply reduced recovery and profit.
Test a robust heavy-products configuration with moderate stage counts and duties: recover the high-value octane/nonane cut, then split it into two premium pure products.
Restore the best C3-recovery design after the heavy-products test proved unprofitable; use its exact settings as the baseline for further targeted optimization.
Test a modest further increase in feed-column stripping to recover the remaining C3s from the worthless bottoms while preserving the inexpensive downstream split.
The C3 blend is already nearly fully monetized, so reduce the dominant feed-column capital and reflux cost while retaining its successful stripping rate.
Restore the best profitable two-column C3-blend design after the reduced feed-column settings eliminated all saleable product.

The ethane column is inexpensive but its overhead still contains roughly 150 mol/s of valuable C3s. Increase its boil-up to drive those C3s into the saleable blend without enlarging the costly feed column.
Restore the best two-column C3-blend design before testing cheaper ways to retain its separation.
Reduce stripping in the inexpensive ethane/C3 column so fewer valuable C3s are carried overhead, while retaining enough reflux for a clean ethane rejection.
Restore the best valid design before pursuing a different, cost-effective product split.
Trim the dominant feed-column reflux duty slightly while preserving its sharp C3/C4 split and the existing C3-blend column.
Restore the best C3-blend design exactly, then use the remaining budget to tune only its dominant feed-column cost while preserving saleability.
Restore the best valid C3-blend design so subsequent trials start from the known profitable operating point rather than the current unsaleable design.
Add a moderately sized C4/C5 splitter below the feed column to monetize the large isobutane/n-butane blend while keeping its cost well below the main column.
Sharpen the C4/C5 split and recover more of the butanes overhead: the potential C4 blend is worth roughly $247M/yr, so a cleaner split can justify a larger second column.
Return to the profitable C3-blend base and test a sharper C4/C5 split: more rectification and boil-up should bring the butane blend above 95% while retaining enough margin over the added column cost.
Lower the C4/C5 column pressure and double its stages to exploit better relative volatility and sharpen the split without increasing boil-up; the aim is a saleable C4 blend at manageable duty.
Restore the profitable base and increase boil-up in the inexpensive ethane/C3 column to recover more of the valuable C3 blend from its overhead.
Restore the best valid design before using the remaining budget on targeted improvements.
Test a direct butane-over-C5 split with enough rectification for C4 blend purity, while using moderate boil-up to keep the incremental column cost low.
Restore the best valid C3-blend design; the direct C4/C5 split is too expensive and destroys profitability.
Monetize the valuable heavy end with an easy C7/C8 split followed by an octane/nonane split; both cuts have wide volatility gaps and should be much cheaper than recovering the C4 blend.
Restore the profitable C3-blend base and reduce the dominant feed column's size and reflux; the current split has ample C3 recovery, so modestly cheaper operation may retain blend purity.
Restore the proven C3-blend design; the reduced feed-column settings are uneconomic, so return to the best valid baseline before testing heavy-product recovery.
Test a moderate pressure reduction on both C3 columns; better relative volatility may preserve the blend split while reducing stage and energy requirements.
Restore the best valid C3-blend design before testing targeted heavy-product recovery with modest columns.
Recover high-purity nonane directly from the heavy bottoms with one moderate low-pressure column; this avoids the extra cost of first concentrating the C8/C9 cut.
Restore the best valid C3-blend design; the direct nonane recovery test is uneconomic, so use the remaining budget for targeted improvements.
Improve ethane/C3 separation in the inexpensive second column to recover more of the C3 blend currently lost overhead, while leaving the costly feed split unchanged.
Test heat integration on the dominant feed column: its high-pressure condenser should be hotter than the low-pressure reboiler, potentially saving enough energy to justify the second shell.
Revert the uneconomic double-effect test to the proven C3-blend design; no heat link is possible with these reboiler temperatures.
Reduce the inexpensive C3 column's severity to keep more C3 in the blend while retaining at least 95% C3 purity; the current sharp ethane split sacrifices about 150 mol/s of valuable C3 overhead.
The blend has about 2.4% purity headroom and the overhead still contains substantial C3. Reduce the small column's reflux and boil-up to recover more C3 while lowering its operating cost.
Restore the best valid C3-blend design after the excessive reduction in the second column's severity; use the remaining solves for controlled recovery and cost improvements.
Test a mild pressure reduction only on the dominant feed column, leaving the profitable blend-polishing column unchanged; improved relative volatility may reduce its very large energy cost.
Restore the best valid two-column C3-blend design after the uneconomic feed-column pressure reduction.
The feed split is already sharp; test whether five fewer stages preserve C3 recovery and blend purity while cutting the dominant column's capital cost.
Restore the best valid two-column C3-blend design after the reduced-stage feed column proved uneconomic.
Test a modest reduction in the dominant column's reflux while holding its boil-up fixed; the C3 split may remain sharp enough for the blend while materially reducing energy cost.
Restore the best valid C3-blend design after the lower feed-column reflux caused an uneconomic split.
Trim only the small column's boil-up to reduce overhead C3 losses while allowing a controlled amount of ethane into the 95% C3 blend.
Restore the best valid two-column C3-blend design; the latest boil-up trim made the blend too impure and is uneconomic.
Add a warm C4/C5 split below the existing profitable design; the C4 blend can be sold without separating isobutane from n-butane, adding substantial revenue at modest cost.
Sharpen the C4/C5 cut so the tops reach the 95% C4-blend threshold; the added C4 revenue can justify a larger warm column, unlike the current unpurified tops.
The C4 blend is still contaminated by C5; increase stages and internal traffic to push pentanes into the bottoms and recover the large C4-blend value.
Test a direct nonane bottoms cut: n-nonane is worth about $404M/yr pure, so one warm column could outperform the C3-blend plant without recovering the lighter products.
Restore the best valid C3-blend design; the direct nonane cut gives no sellable product and is uneconomic.
Test a sharper warm nonane bottoms cut with enough stages and boil-up to reach saleable purity; this avoids the costly refrigerated C3 split and targets the feed's second-largest product value.
Restore the best valid C3-blend design before spending the remaining solves on targeted warm-bottoms opportunities.
Replace the refrigerated C3 flowsheet with two warm columns: recover an octane/nonane bottoms cut, then split it into two high-value pure products.
Restore the best valid two-column C3-blend design; the warm octane/nonane sequence did not produce saleable products.
Target the high-value C4 blend from the existing warm bottoms with a sharper but still moderate C4/C5 split; a saleable tops stream would add roughly $240M/yr.
Restore the best valid two-column C3-blend design before using the remaining solves on targeted refinements.
The C3 purification column is inexpensive but sends substantial propylene and propane overhead with ethane. Increase its stages and reflux to recover more C3 blend while retaining 95% purity.
Increase rectification in the inexpensive C3 column to reduce the large propylene/propane loss overhead while preserving the C3 blend.
Reduce boil-up in the inexpensive C3 column to keep more propylene and propane in the saleable bottoms while allowing minor ethane leakage within blend purity.
Return to the best C3-blend design and use an intermediate boil-up to limit ethane in the bottoms without losing excessive C3 overhead.
Restore the best C3 recovery column and reduce the expensive feed column's stages and reflux; its bottoms are unsold, so only C3 recovery and limiting C4 leakage matter.
Restore the best valid C3-blend design; the reduced feed-column rectification made the C3 blend unsaleable.
The C3 column has substantial ethane-leakage margin in its saleable bottoms, so test fewer stages to reduce capital while retaining blend purity and recovery.
Trim the feed column's reflux modestly to reduce its dominant energy cost while retaining the C4 rejection needed for a saleable C3 blend.
Restore the best valid C3-blend design after the feed-column reflux reduction proved uneconomic.
Recover the valuable C4 blend from the warm bottoms with a compact C4/C5 split; modest stages and reflux should limit cost while keeping C5 contamination below 5%.
The C4 blend is worth roughly $300M/yr, so test a stronger C4/C5 split: the compact column lost too much C4 overhead yet still carried excessive C5 into the tops.
Restore the best valid C3-blend design after the C4 recovery column failed to cover its cost.
The warm heavy bottoms contain $404M/yr of n-nonane. Test a moderate octane/nonane finishing split to recover it without adding low-value intermediate separations.
Restore the best C3-blend design; the nonane finishing column's high reboiler duty eliminated essentially all profit.
The feed column dominates cost through its large cold reflux duty. Add rectification stages so reflux can be reduced while preserving the C3/C4 split and blend purity.
Restore the best valid C3-blend design after the high-stage feed-column trial failed to converge.
The feed column’s boil-up is a major cost and the C3 product has purity margin. Test a modest boil-up reduction while retaining enough C4 rejection and C3 recovery.
Restore the best design and reduce the C3 column’s reflux: its ethane-free blend has ample purity margin, so this should cut condenser and reboiler duty without losing revenue.
Restore the best valid design before the final optimization trials; the reduced C3 reflux lowered reward.
Test a liquid C4 side draw from the existing warm feed column. A saleable C4 blend could add about $300M/yr without another column, while preserving the proven C3 product.
Restore the best C3-blend design and shorten the ethane-removal column. Ethane is much lighter than propylene, so 50 stages should retain blend purity while reducing capital cost.
The C3 blend has a modest purity margin and the feed column dominates cost. Test a small reflux reduction while retaining the proven 30-stage split and boil-up.
Restore the best valid C3-blend design after the feed-column reflux reduction sharply increased total cost and eliminated product value.
Shorten the easy ethane/C3 split further to reduce capital and duties while checking that the C3 blend remains above 95%.
Test a moderate feed pressure reduction: easier C3/C4 relative volatility may cut the very large feed-column duties enough to outweigh colder condenser temperatures.
Restore the best C3-blend design after the pressure reduction sharply degraded separation and product value.
The ethane/C3 split is easy and the blend has adequate purity. Shorten this small column further to reduce capital and utility costs while preserving the proven feed split.
Continue shortening the small, easy ethane/C3 splitter to reduce its cost while preserving the C3 blend above 95%.

Restore the best design, then make a small feed-column boil-up reduction with the cheaper 15-stage ethane splitter. This should lower the dominant reboiler cost while using the small remaining C3-blend purity margin.
Restore the best design and modestly shorten the dominant feed column. The C3/C4 split is sharp, so two fewer stages may reduce capital cost without losing blend purity.
Restore the best design and test one fewer stage in the small ethane/C3 splitter, seeking a marginal capital saving without losing blend purity.

Restore the best 15-stage ethane splitter and increase boil-up modestly. The overhead currently rejects valuable C3 material with the ethane; a slightly smaller overhead could raise C3 recovery and revenue for little extra utility cost.
Restore the best design and make a small reduction in the ethane splitter boil-up. This may recover more C3 product and reduce duty while keeping ethane contamination below the blend limit.
Restore the best design and make a small reflux reduction in the easy ethane/C3 splitter. This should cut duty while retaining the C3 blend's purity margin.
Restore the best valid design; recent small utility and stage changes have not improved reward, and the remaining solves are best preserved.
Make a very small reduction in the dominant feed column's reflux. The C3 blend is near its purity limit, so this tests whether meaningful duty savings are available without losing saleability.
Restore the best valid design after the feed-column reflux reduction caused the C3 blend to fail specification.
With the C3 design at a local optimum, use the remaining solves to test whether the large, easily split C4 fraction in the bottoms can be sold as a C4 blend for a meaningful net gain.

Restore the best C3 design and test a lower boil-up in the bottoms column. This should reject C5 and heavier material to the bottoms, allowing the overhead to sell as a C4 blend while also reducing reboiler duty.

Restore the best C3 design and test a substantially lower bottoms boil-up. The C4/C5 boiling-point gap is large, so this may reject enough C5 to make the overhead a saleable C4 blend while retaining useful C4 recovery.

Restore the best design and make one serious attempt to recover the valuable C4 blend. Much stronger C4/C5 fractionation should reject pentanes while the moderate boil-up retains enough butane overhead.
Restore the best valid design. The final C4-recovery attempts remain uneconomic and do not meet blend purity, so the proven C3 configuration should be preserved.
Test one fewer stage in the dominant feed column while preserving its operating ratios. A small capital saving would be worthwhile if the C3 blend remains above specification.
Restore the best valid design after the one-stage reduction slightly reduced reward. Remaining alternatives have been uneconomic, so preserve the proven optimum.
Preserve the best valid design (reward 0.270). Remaining trials have not improved the C3-blend configuration, and C4 recovery was uneconomic.
